{{Short description|Geometric formula for finding the ratio in which a line segment is divided by a point}}
{{Orphan|date=March 2022}}
In [[coordinate geometry]], the ''' Section formula''' is a formula used to find the ratio in which a line segment is divided by a point internally or externally.<ref name=":1">{{Citation|last1=Clapham|first1=Christopher|chapter=section formulae|date=2014-09-18|chapter-url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780199679591.001.0001/acref-9780199679591-e-2546|title=The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Mathematics|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=en|doi=10.1093/acref/9780199679591.001.0001|isbn=978-0-19-967959-1|access-date=2020-10-30|last2=Nicholson|first2=James|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> It is used to find out the [[centroid]], [[incenter]] and [[excenter]]s of a [[triangle]]. In [[physics]], it is used to find the [[center of mass]] of systems, [[equilibrium point]]s, etc.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Section Formula {{!}} Brilliant Math & Science Wiki|url=https://brilliant.org/wiki/section-formula/|access-date=2020-10-16|website=brilliant.org|language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Coordinate Geometry | url=https://ncert.nic.in/ncerts/l/jemh107.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160626111706/http://www.ncert.nic.in/ncerts/l/jemh107.pdf | archive-date=2016-06-26 | access-date=2020-10-16 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Aggarwal|first=R.S.|title=Secondary School Mathematics for Class 10|publisher=Bharti Bhawan Publishers & Distributors (1 January 2020)|isbn=978-9388704519}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Sharma|first=R.D.|title=Mathematics for Class 10|publisher=Dhanpat Rai Publication (1 January 2020)|isbn=978-8194192640}}</ref>

== Internal divisions ==
[[File:Internal division.png|thumb|Internal division with section formula]]
If point P (lying on AB) divides the line segment AB joining the points <math>\mathrm{A}(x_1,y_1)</math> and <math>\mathrm{B}(x_2,y_2)</math> in the ratio m:n, then

<math> P = \left(\frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n},\frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}\right)</math><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Loney|first=S L|title=The Elements of Coordinate Geometry (Part-1)}}</ref>

The ratio m:n can also be written as <math>m/n:1</math>, or <math>k:1</math>, where <math>k=m/n</math>. So, the coordinates of point <math>P</math> dividing the line segment joining the points <math>\mathrm{A}(x_1,y_1)</math> and <math>\mathrm{B}(x_2,y_2)</math> are:

<math>\left(\frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}\right) </math>

<math>=\left(\frac{\frac{m}{n}x_2 +x_1}{\frac{m}{n}+1},\frac{\frac{m}{n}y_2 +y_1}{\frac{m}{n}+1} \right )</math>

<math>=\left ( \frac{kx_2 +x_1}{k +1},\frac{ky_2 + y_1}{k +1} \right )</math><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

Similarly, the ratio can also be written as <math>k:(1-k)</math>, and the coordinates of P are <math>((1-k)x_1 + kx_2, (1-k)y_1 + ky_2) </math>.<ref name=":1" />

=== Proof ===
Triangles <math>PAQ\sim BPC </math>. 
:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{AP}{BP}=\frac{AQ}{CP}=\frac{PQ}{BC}\\
\frac{m}{n}=\frac{x-x_1}{x_2-x}=\frac{y-y_1}{y_2-y}\\
mx_2-mx=nx-nx_1,my_2-my=ny-ny_1\\
mx+nx=mx_2+nx_1, my+ny=my_2+ny_1\\
(m+n)x=mx_2+nx_1, (m+n)y=my_2+ny_1\\
x=\frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, y=\frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}\\
\end{align}
</math>

== External divisions ==
[[File:External division.png|thumb|External division with section formula]]
If a point P (lying on the extension of AB) divides AB in the ratio m:n then

<math>P = \left(\dfrac{mx_2 - nx_1}{m - n}, \dfrac{my_2 - ny_1}{m - n}\right)</math><ref name=":0" />

=== Proof ===
Triangles <math>PAC\sim PBD </math> (Let C and D be two points where A & P and B & P intersect respectively).
Therefore ∠ACP = ∠BDP 
 
:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{AB}{BP}=\frac{AC}{BD}=\frac{PC}{PD}\\
\frac{m}{n}=\frac{x-x_1}{x-x_2}=\frac{y-y_1}{y-y_2}\\
mx-mx_2=nx-nx_1,my-my_2=ny-ny_1\\
mx-nx=mx_2-nx_1, my-ny=my_2-ny_1\\
(m-n)x=mx_2-nx_1, (m-n)y=my_2-ny_1\\
x=\frac{mx_2 - nx_1}{m - n}, y=\frac{my_2 - ny_1}{m - n}\\
\end{align}
</math>

== Midpoint formula ==
{{Main|Midpoint}}
The midpoint of a line segment divides it internally in the ratio <math display="inline">1:1</math>. Applying the Section formula for internal division:<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

<math display="block">P = \left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right)</math>

=== Derivation ===
<math>P = \left(\dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, \dfrac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}\right) </math>

<math>= \left ( \frac{1\cdot x_1 + 1\cdot x_2}{1+1},\frac{1 \cdot y_1 + 1\cdot y_2}{1+1} \right )</math>

<math>=\left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right)</math>

==Centroid==
[[File:Centroid.svg|thumb|Centroid of a triangle]]
The centroid of a triangle is the intersection of the [[Medians of a triangle|medians]] and divides each median in the ratio <math display="inline">2:1</math>. Let the vertices of the triangle be <math>A(x_1, y_1)</math>, <math display="inline">B(x_2, y_2)</math> and <math display="inline">C(x_3, y_3)</math>. So, a median from point A will intersect BC at <math display="inline">\left(\frac{x_2 + x_3}{2}, \frac{y_2 + y_3}{2}\right)</math>. 
Using the section formula, the centroid becomes:
:<math display="block">
\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3},\frac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3} \right)</math>

== In three dimensions ==
Let A and B be two points with [[Cartesian coordinates]] ''(x<sub>1</sub>, y<sub>1</sub>, z<sub>1</sub>)'' and ''(x<sub>2</sub>, y<sub>2</sub>, z<sub>2</sub>)'' and P be a point on the line through A and B. If <math>AP:PB =m:n</math>. Then the section formula gives the coordinates of P as

:<math>\left ( \frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m +n} ,\frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m+n}, \frac{mz_2 + nz_1}{m+n} \right )</math><ref name=":1"/>

If, instead, P is a point on the line such that <math>AP:PB = k:1-k</math>, its coordinates are <math>((1-k)x_1 + kx_2, (1-k)y_1 + ky_2, (1-k)z_1 + kz_2)</math>.<ref name=":1"/>

== In vectors ==
The position vector of a point P dividing the line segment joining the points A and B whose position vectors are <math>\vec{a}</math> and <math>\vec{b}</math>

# in the ratio <math>m:n</math> internally, is given by <math>\frac{n\vec{a} + m\vec{b}}{m+n}</math><ref name=":5">{{Cite web | title=Vector Algebra | url=https://ncert.nic.in/ncerts/l/leep210.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161213040342/http://ncert.nic.in/ncerts/l/leep210.pdf | archive-date=2016-12-13 | access-date=2020-10-30 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":1" />
# in the ratio <math>m:n</math> externally, is given by <math>\frac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m-n}</math><ref name=":5" />
